Well, my wife actually pushed me to come in, but... I guess the main thing is that I just, I don't know, I've completely stopped caring about everything I used to look forward to. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like... take my fishing gear, for example. It’s just sitting untouched out in the garage. Usually, by this time of year, I'd have all the tackle boxes sorted, checking the lines, getting ready to head out to the lake for the weekend, you know? I even bought this expensive new reel a few months ago and it’s literally still in the shipping box. It's just gathering dust. 

And my woodshop out there, too. I’m a construction manager, so I’m around building sites all day, but doing the fine woodworking at home, making cabinets and furniture, that used to be my escape. Now? Just the thought of walking out there and turning on a saw feels like this massive, impossible chore. I look at the tools and I just feel absolutely nothing. 

And it's not even just the projects... it's with my kids, too. They keep setting up the board to try and get me to play chess with them after dinner. I taught them how to play, we used to get really into it and have these big tournaments at the kitchen table, but lately... I sit down with them, and I'm just going through the motions. I move the pieces, but I don't care what happens. I'm just staring at the board waiting for the game to be over so I can just be done with it. It’s just this total blankness where all my interests used to be, and I just can't seem to shake it no matter how hard I try to force myself.

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... it’s been a while. It’s been about a year and seven months, actually. I can pinpoint it pretty exactly because that’s right around the time my wife started having all her health problems, and that just... well, it changed everything at home. I figured, okay, I’ll just leave the fishing gear in the garage for a few weeks, I’ll close up the woodshop until things settle down and we get a handle on her health. But then... even when things did start to stabilize a bit with her, and we got into a new sort of rhythm at home, I just never went back to any of it. The time was there again, but the drive was just completely gone. 

So yeah, it's been a year and seven months of just... walking past the garage and feeling nothing. It’s like a switch flipped when her health issues started and the house changed, and I just haven't been able to flip it back on since, no matter how much time passes.

Sad? I mean... not really. Not sad, no. It’s funny you ask it that way, because my wife actually asked me the exact same thing a few weeks ago. She asked if I was feeling sad, and I really had to sit and think about it. Because when I think of being sad, I think of... you know, crying, or feeling like your heart is heavy, or grieving. But this... whatever this is that’s been going on since then... it’s not sadness. It’s more like... my emotional tank is just completely bone dry. 

Like, just last week at the site, we had this massive issue with a concrete pour. The weather turned unexpectedly, the mix got messed up, and it was a total disaster that set us back thousands of dollars and threw the whole project schedule off. A couple of years ago, that would have wrecked me for the week. I would have been really down, stressed, feeling miserable about it. But I just stood there in the mud looking at this ruined foundation, and I felt absolutely nothing. No sadness, no frustration, just... totally flat. 

It’s like that with everything now. I wake up, I go to work, I come home, and it’s just one long, continuous flatline. I almost wish I *was* sad, to be completely honest with you, because at least if you’re sad, it means you still care about something, right? It means you’re still reacting to the world around you. But I’m not reacting. I'm just sort of... existing. Going through the motions. So no, I wouldn't say I feel down or sad most of the time. I just don't really feel much of anything at all.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Anxious? Worried? No, not really. I mean, I guess you'd think I would be, right? With my wife's health stuff, and the kids, and that concrete disaster at work I was telling you about... on paper, I should be a nervous wreck. A couple of years ago, I definitely would have been. I used to be the kind of guy who would lie awake at night running through the project schedules in my head, worrying about whether the drywall guys were going to show up on time, or if the permits for the new subdivision were going to clear the city council. I was always sort of... humming with that low-level stress, you know? 

But now? It's just like I was saying about not feeling sad. The worry just isn't there. It's like the part of my brain that's supposed to sound the alarm when things go wrong has just been completely disconnected. When my wife had a follow-up appointment last month, and they were running all these tests, she was pacing the floor, totally beside herself with anxiety. And I was just sitting in the waiting room chair, staring at an old magazine, feeling absolutely nothing. I knew I *should* be worried, I knew it was a big deal, but I just couldn't muster up the energy to actually care. 

Even at the site, when things go sideways—and they always go sideways in construction—I don't get that spike of adrenaline or panic anymore. My foreman came running up to me on Tuesday yelling about how the plumbing rough-in was completely wrong and we'd have to tear out a week's worth of work. He was sweating, totally panicked. And I just looked at him and said, "Okay, tear it out then." I didn't care. I didn't worry about the budget, I didn't worry about the timeline. I just felt that same flat, empty feeling. So no, anxiety really isn't an issue for me right now. I almost wish I could feel worried, just to feel something.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Guilty? Yeah. Yeah, I do. All the time, actually. It's... it's heavy. Like, I know I just said I don't feel much of anything, but the guilt is... it's loud. It's really loud. 

I just... I keep thinking about how I'm failing everybody. I mean, my wife, right? She's been through the wringer with her health, and she needs me to be the rock, the guy who supports her and keeps the family going. And what am I doing? I'm sitting there like a zombie, barely eating the dinner she makes, not even reacting when she's terrified about her test results. I feel this immense guilt that I can't just snap out of it and be the husband she deserves. I feel like I'm letting her down every single day. 

And then there's the kids. Like I said before, I sit there playing chess with my son, and I'm just waiting for it to be over. What kind of father does that? He's a great kid, he just wants to spend time with his dad, and I can't even give him that without wishing I was somewhere else, or just... nowhere. I look at them and I just think about how I'm failing them, how they deserve a dad who's actually present, who actually cares.

And it doesn't stop at home, either. It bleeds into work. I'm the manager. I'm supposed to be leading the crews, keeping everything on track. But lately... if anything goes wrong, and I mean *anything*, I just take it all on myself. Like, if a subcontractor misses an appointment, or there's a cost overrun because of material prices, or even if a guy forgets his hard hat and it's a safety issue... I don't just think, "Oh, that's a problem we need to fix." I think, "This is my fault. This proves I'm useless." 

I just sit in my truck sometimes and think about how the guys at work would probably be so much better off if someone else was in charge. Someone who actually cared if a pour got ruined or if the plumbing was wrong. I feel like an imposter, just taking up space, dragging everyone down with me. Every little mistake, every setback on the site, every time my wife looks at me with that worried expression... it all just piles up into this mountain of guilt. I just feel like a complete and utter failure to everyone who depends on me.

I... man, that's a heavy question to answer. I guess... I mean, I wouldn't say I'm sitting at home at the kitchen table plotting out a way to do it, you know? I don't have a plan or anything like that. But... well, it goes back to what I was saying about the guilt and the job and just feeling so completely useless to everybody.

I have to be the first one at the site to unlock the gates and get the day's schedules ready before the crews start rolling in. So I'm out of the house by 5:00. It's pitch black out. My wife and the kids are still dead to the world, the neighborhood is completely silent, and I just get in my truck and hit the highway. I don't even turn the radio on anymore. It's just me in the dark for a forty-five-minute commute. 

And on those early drives, before anyone else is even awake... it's just so quiet in the cab, and my brain just starts running through everything I'm doing wrong. And I catch myself staring at the headlights on the asphalt, or looking at the concrete pillars for the overpasses coming up, and I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I just didn't make it there. If I just didn't show up to the site at all. 

I'll be doing sixty-five, seventy miles an hour, and I look at the drop-offs on the side of the highway, and this thought just sort of washes over me about how simple it would be to just... jerk the wheel. Just a couple of inches to the right. It would look like an accident. People would think I fell asleep or blew a tire, and my wife would get the life insurance, and she wouldn't have to deal with this empty shell of a husband anymore, and the guys at work could get a manager who actually cares. It just feels like it would solve everyone's problems.

And honestly, Doc... sometimes the thought of steering off the road like that... it really scares me. It scares me because of how much sense it makes to me in those moments. It feels way too close. Like the barrier between just having the thought and actually letting my hands do it is getting thinner every morning. I'll get to the site and park the truck, and I'll just sit there gripping the steering wheel until my knuckles are white, just trying to shake the thought out of my head before my foreman pulls up. So... yeah. I guess I have been wishing I was dead. I just haven't said it out loud until right now.

It’s hard to explain, but it’s like... take my fishing gear, for example. It’s just sitting untouched out in the garage. Usually, by this time of year, I'd have all the tackle boxes sorted, checking the lines, getting ready to head out to the lake for the weekend, you know? I even bought this expensive new reel a few months ago and it’s literally still in the shipping box. It's just gathering dust. \n\nAnd my woodshop out there, too. I’m a construction manager, so I’m around building sites all day, but doing the fine woodworking at home, making cabinets and furniture, that used to be my escape. Now? Just the thought of walking out there and turning on a saw feels like this massive, impossible chore. I look at the tools and I just feel absolutely nothing. \n\nAnd it's not even just the projects... it's with my kids, too. They keep setting up the board to try and get me to play chess with them after dinner. I taught them how to play, we used to get really into it and have these big tournaments at the kitchen table, but lately... I sit down with them, and I'm just going through the motions. I move the pieces, but I don't care what happens. I'm just staring at the board waiting for the game to be over so I can just be done with it. It’s just this total blankness where all my interests used to be, and I just can't seem to shake it no matter how hard I try to force myself.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, with no interest in the things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... it’s been a while. It’s been about a year and seven months, actually. I can pinpoint it pretty exactly because that’s right around the time my wife started having all her health problems, and that just... well, it changed everything at home. Completely turned our lives upside down. \n\nBefore that, you know, we had our routine. I had my shop time on the weekends, we’d do the chess tournaments with the kids after dinner... but when she got sick, everything just shifted. Suddenly the whole dynamic of the house was different. I was picking up a lot more of the slack, which, you know, I’m happy to do, she’s my wife and I love her, but... it was a huge adjustment for all of us. \n\nAt first, I just thought I was putting my hobbies on hold because I was busy and stressed. I figured, okay, I’ll just leave the fishing gear in the garage for a few weeks, I’ll close up the woodshop until things settle down and we get a handle on her health. But then... even when things did start to stabilize a bit with her, and we got into a new sort of rhythm at home, I just never went back to any of it. The time was there again, but the drive was just completely gone. \n\nSo yeah, it's been a year and seven months of just... walking past the garage and feeling nothing. It’s like a switch flipped when her health issues started and the house changed, and I just haven't been able to flip it back on since, no matter how much time passes.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time since you lost interest in your hobbies?\n\nPatient: Sad? I mean... not really. Not sad, no. It’s funny you ask it that way, because my wife actually asked me the exact same thing a few weeks ago. She asked if I was feeling sad, and I really had to sit and think about it. Because when I think of being sad, I think of... you know, crying, or feeling like your heart is heavy, or grieving. Like when she first got sick, I was definitely sad then. I remember sitting in my truck outside the clinic just bawling my eyes out. But this... whatever this is that’s been going on since then... it’s not sadness. It’s more like... my emotional tank is just completely bone dry. \n\nLike, just last week at the site, we had this massive issue with a concrete pour. The weather turned unexpectedly, the mix got messed up, and it was a total disaster that set us back thousands of dollars and threw the whole project schedule off. A couple of years ago, that would have wrecked me for the week. I would have been really down, stressed, feeling miserable about it. But I just stood there in the mud looking at this ruined foundation, and I felt absolutely nothing. No sadness, no frustration, just... totally flat. \n\nIt’s like that with everything now. I wake up, I go to work, I come home, and it’s just one long, continuous flatline. I almost wish I *was* sad, to be completely honest with you, because at least if you’re sad, it means you still care about something, right? It means you’re still reacting to the world around you. But I’m not reacting. I'm just sort of... existing. Going through the motions. So no, I wouldn't say I feel down or sad most of the time. I just don't really feel much of anything at all.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy things like eating your favorite foods or spending time with loved ones?\n\nPatient: Well, as far as spending time with loved ones goes... like I was saying with the kids and the chess games, I'm physically in the room with them, but I'm not really *with* them, you know? I'm just waiting for it to be over. \n\nAnd as for food... it's funny you bring that up, actually, because my wife and I were just having a whole thing about this the other night. She makes this incredible baked ziti, usually my absolute favorite thing in the world, but lately... I don't know, most days food just literally tastes like cardboard to me. It really doesn't matter what it is or how much I used to love it. I'll wake up in the morning and just completely skip breakfast, which is crazy for me. \n\nAnd you have to understand, being a construction manager, I'm out on a job site all day long. I'm on my feet, walking through the mud, climbing around framing, dealing with the crews—I'm burning a ton of energy. By all rights, I should be absolutely ravenous by the time I get home. But I sit down for dinner, even when she makes my favorites, and I just... I just pick at it. I push the food around my plate and maybe manage a few bites, but chewing and swallowing just feels like this massive chore. \n\nIt's actually starting to show, too, which is another thing my wife is stressed about. My work jeans are getting really loose. I've had to bring my belt in a couple of notches recently, and I haven't been trying to lose weight or go on a diet or anything like that. It's just happening on its own because I can barely force myself to eat. The enjoyment of it is just completely gone.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or worried about things that are happening in your life?\n\nPatient: Anxious? Worried? No, not really. I mean, I guess you'd think I would be, right? With my wife's health stuff, and the kids, and that concrete disaster at work I was telling you about... on paper, I should be a nervous wreck. A couple of years ago, I definitely would have been. I used to be the kind of guy who would lie awake at night running through the project schedules in my head, worrying about whether the drywall guys were going to show up on time, or if the permits for the new subdivision were going to clear the city council. I was always sort of... humming with that low-level stress, you know? \n\nBut now? It's just like I was saying about not feeling sad. The worry just isn't there. It's like the part of my brain that's supposed to sound the alarm when things go wrong has just been completely disconnected. When my wife had a follow-up appointment last month, and they were running all these tests, she was pacing the floor, totally beside herself with anxiety. And I was just sitting in the waiting room chair, staring at an old magazine, feeling absolutely nothing. I knew I *should* be worried, I knew it was a big deal, but I just couldn't muster up the energy to actually care. \n\nEven at the site, when things go sideways—and they always go sideways in construction—I don't get that spike of adrenaline or panic anymore. My foreman came running up to me on Tuesday yelling about how the plumbing rough-in was completely wrong and we'd have to tear out a week's worth of work. He was sweating, totally panicked. And I just looked at him and said, \"Okay, tear it out then.\" I didn't care. I didn't worry about the budget, I didn't worry about the timeline. I just felt that same flat, empty feeling. So no, anxiety really isn't an issue for me right now. I almost wish I could feel worried, just to feel something.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty about anything?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Yeah. Yeah, I do. All the time, actually. It's... it's heavy. Like, I know I just said I don't feel much of anything, but the guilt is... it's loud. It's really loud. \n\nI just... I keep thinking about how I'm failing everybody. I mean, my wife, right? She's been through the wringer with her health, and she needs me to be the rock, the guy who supports her and keeps the family going. And what am I doing? I'm sitting there like a zombie, barely eating the dinner she makes, not even reacting when she's terrified about her test results. I feel this immense guilt that I can't just snap out of it and be the husband she deserves. I feel like I'm letting her down every single day. \n\nAnd then there's the kids. Like I said before, I sit there playing chess with my son, and I'm just waiting for it to be over. What kind of father does that? He's a great kid, he just wants to spend time with his dad, and I can't even give him that without wishing I was somewhere else, or just... nowhere. I look at them and I just think about how I'm failing them, how they deserve a dad who's actually present, who actually cares.\n\nAnd it doesn't stop at home, either. It bleeds into work. I'm the manager. I'm supposed to be leading the crews, keeping everything on track. But lately... if anything goes wrong, and I mean *anything*, I just take it all on myself. Like, if a subcontractor misses an appointment, or there's a cost overrun because of material prices, or even if a guy forgets his hard hat and it's a safety issue... I don't just think, \"Oh, that's a problem we need to fix.\" I think, \"This is my fault. This proves I'm useless.\" \n\nI just sit in my truck sometimes and think about how the guys at work would probably be so much better off if someone else was in charge. Someone who actually cared if a pour got ruined or if the plumbing was wrong. I feel like an imposter, just taking up space, dragging everyone down with me. Every little mistake, every setback on the site, every time my wife looks at me with that worried expression... it all just piles up into this mountain of guilt. I just feel like a complete and utter failure to everyone who depends on me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you were dead?\n\nPatient: I... man, that's a heavy question to answer. I guess... I mean, I wouldn't say I'm sitting at home at the kitchen table plotting out a way to do it, you know? I don't have a plan or anything like that. But... well, it goes back to what I was saying about the guilt and the job and just feeling so completely useless to everybody. \n\nMy alarm goes off at 4:30 every morning, which is pretty standard for my line of work. I have to be the first one at the site to unlock the gates and get the day's schedules ready before the crews start rolling in. So I'm out of the house by 5:00. It's pitch black out. My wife and the kids are still dead to the world, the neighborhood is completely silent, and I just get in my truck and hit the highway. I don't even turn the radio on anymore. It's just me in the dark for a forty-five-minute commute. \n\nAnd on those early drives, before anyone else is even awake... it's just so quiet in the cab, and my brain just starts running through everything I'm doing wrong. People would think I fell asleep or blew a tire, and my wife would get the life insurance, and she wouldn't have to deal with this empty shell of a husband anymore, and the guys at work could get a manager who actually cares. It just feels like it would solve everyone's problems.\n\nAnd honestly, Doc... sometimes the thought of steering off the road like that... it really scares me. It scares me because of how much sense it makes to me in those moments. It feels way too close. Like the barrier between just having the thought and actually letting my hands do it is getting thinner every morning. Tired? Yeah. Man, tired doesn't even really begin to cover it. It’s... it’s this deep, bone-weary kind of exhaustion that just never goes away, no matter what I do. 

Like I was telling you about getting up at 4:30 and driving in in the dark... by the time it hits, what, 10:00 AM? Midmorning? I already feel like I’ve worked an entire twelve-hour shift. We're doing this three-story commercial build right now, and just... just walking the project, trying to keep up with the crew, it takes absolutely everything out of me. 

When I have to climb the temporary stairs to check the upper floors, my legs just... they don't want to move. It literally feels like my body is carrying wet concrete. You know how heavy that is? Just dragging myself up one step at a time, feeling like I'm hauling around a hundred extra pounds of sludge in my veins. I used to run up and down those ladders, no problem, constantly on the move, checking on five different things at once. Now, I get to the top of a flight of stairs and I have to just stand there, pretending I'm studying a blueprint or checking an email on my phone, just so the guys don't see me struggling and so I can try to find the energy to take another step. 

It's every single day. I go to bed exhausted, I wake up exhausted, and by the first coffee break, I'm just completely spent. It's just this heavy, dragging feeling all the time, like gravity is pulling on me twice as hard as everyone else.

Yeah, sleep is... it's a whole other nightmare, honestly. You would think, with how bone-tired I was just telling you I am all day, dragging myself up those temporary stairs and feeling like I'm full of wet concrete... you'd think I would just pass out the second my head hits the pillow, right? My wife is sleeping right next to me, completely peaceful, and I'm just staring at the ceiling, watching the shadows from the streetlights, just waiting and waiting until it’s finally time to get up and drive to the site. 

It's maddening, Doc. Because I know I need the rest. My body is screaming for it. But lying there at 3:30 in the morning, when the whole house is dead quiet... every single thing I've done wrong, every failure, it all just magnifies in the dark. I try changing positions, I try flipping the pillow, but nothing works. I'm literally just sitting there, faking a smile, waiting for the game to be over so I can go stare at the ceiling in the bedroom. Focusing? Man, it's... it's embarrassing, honestly. It really is. Because I used to be sharp. You have to be, in my line of work. When you're managing a site, there are a million moving parts, and I used to keep all the schedules, all the different subcontractors—the plumbers, the electricians, the framers—I kept all of it perfectly straight right here in my head. I didn't even need to look at the master clipboard half the time. I just knew exactly who was supposed to be where, what materials they needed, what the timeline was. 

But now? Now it's like my brain is just... it's just packed full of cotton. I can't hold onto a single thought. I'll sit down in the site trailer to check my inbox, and I'll open an email from the architect or a supplier. I'll read the whole thing, top to bottom, and then realize I didn't process a single word. So I have to read it again. And then, I swear to you, I'll have to read the exact same email a third time just to comprehend a basic update about a lumber delivery. It's pathetic. I'm just staring at the screen and the words don't mean anything.

And the meetings are even worse. We have these weekly coordination meetings with the foremen and sometimes the project investors, and I'm supposed to be the guy running them. I'll be right in the middle of talking, right in the middle of a sentence giving instructions, and I'll just... I'll completely forget what I was about to say. The thought just evaporates. And I'm standing there at the head of the table, looking like an absolute idiot, just totally blank, trying to shuffle blueprints around to buy myself time to remember what the hell we were even talking about. 

And then there's the calls I have to make. In construction, you're making a hundred little judgment calls a day, right? Approving a change order, figuring out a workaround if a wall is out of plumb... I used to make those decisions in five minutes, tops. I trusted my experience, I made the call, and we moved on. Now, I just freeze. Somebody asks me a simple question about a pour schedule, and I just freeze up entirely. I'll agonize over a decision I used to make in five minutes, just terrified I'm going to ruin the whole build because I can't trust my own head anymore. It's like I just can't process information, and it's slowing the whole job down.

She's been through the wringer with her health, and she needs me to be the rock, the guy who supports her and keeps the family going. And what am I doing? I'm sitting there like a zombie, barely eating the dinner she makes, not even reacting when she's terrified about her test results. I feel this immense guilt that I can't just snap out of it and be the husband she deserves. I feel like I'm letting her down every single day. \n\nAnd then there's the kids. I'm the manager. I'm supposed to be leading the crews, keeping everything on track. But lately... if anything goes wrong, and I mean *anything*, I just take it all on myself. I don't just think, \"Oh, that's a problem we need to fix.\" I think, \"This is my fault. Someone who actually cared if a pour got ruined or if the plumbing was wrong. I feel like an imposter, just taking up space, dragging everyone down with me. Every little mistake, every setback on the site, every time my wife looks at me with that worried expression... it all just piles up into this mountain of guilt. If I just didn't show up to the site at all. \n\nI'll be doing sixty-five, seventy miles an hour, and I look at the drop-offs on the side of the highway, and this thought just sort of washes over me about how simple it would be to just... jerk the wheel. Weight... yeah, actually. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just noticing it the other morning when I was getting dressed for the site. I haven't stepped on a scale or anything—I don't even know where my wife keeps the scale in the bathroom these days—but I've definitely dropped some weight. And I'm absolutely not trying to. Frequency... man, it's... it's happening more than I'd like to admit. Mostly it's in the mornings. You know, in my line of work, I'm out the door before the sun is even thinking about coming up. I'm usually in my truck by 4:30, maybe 5:00 AM, making the commute out to the current build site. And at that hour, it's just pitch black. The roads are completely empty, no traffic, I don't even have the radio on, it's just me and the headlights cutting through the dark. And it's so quiet. It's on those early drives, before anyone else is awake, that it really hits me. I'll be coming up on this one long stretch of highway, and I just catch myself thinking... thinking it would just be so much easier if I just didn’t make it there. If the drive just ended and I didn't have to show up to the site, didn't have to go back home and face the reality of my wife's health, didn't have to carry all this heavy, dead weight anymore. Just... done. 

And it's not like I have a detailed plan or I'm sitting around writing a note, it's just this... this overwhelming urge to just stop existing. But lately, maybe three or four mornings a week now, it goes a little further than just wishing I'd fade away in my sleep. It really scares me, Doc, because it feels too close. It feels like all it would take is just a two-inch pull on the steering wheel to the right, just letting my hands go slack for three seconds, and it would all be over. I wouldn't have to be tired anymore. I end up gripping the wheel so hard my knuckles turn white just to force myself to stay in the center lane. So, yeah... it's frequent enough that I'm actually terrified of my own morning commute at this point.

Yeah. Yeah, that’s... honestly, that’s becoming a massive problem. It’s every single day, and it's starting to really affect my job. 

You know, being a construction manager, my entire livelihood is basically just managing chaos. I used to be the guy who could keep all the schedules and all the different subcontractors straight right here in my head. I wouldn't even need to look at the master sheet half the time, I just knew where the electricians were supposed to be, when the drywall guys were coming in, who was running behind... I prided myself on being sharp like that. I had to be.

But lately? It’s like my brain is just full of wet concrete. I’ll be sitting in the site trailer, trying to get through my morning catch-up, and I’ll read the exact same email from a supplier three or four times in a row, and I still won't comprehend what it says. The words just sort of float there on the screen. And it’s so embarrassing because we have these morning stand-ups, these meetings with the foremen to go over the day's push, and I'll just completely blank. I'll be standing there in the mud, looking at my guys, and I'll just forget what I was about to say right in the middle of a sentence. I just totally lose it, and I have to pretend I'm just pausing to think. 

And the worst part is the decisions. In this line of work, you have to make calls fast to keep the project moving. Time is money, right? I used to make these routine calls in five minutes, easy. Now? I just freeze over them. I'll stare at a simple change order or try to figure out where to stage a lumber delivery, and I just get entirely paralyzed. I can't weigh the options. I just sit there agonizing over decisions I used to make without a second thought.
